lessons.title: This week's table
lessons.objective: You can read {{team}}'s place in the table and what it needs to achieve.

payload.prompt: If a team is fifth with four games left and {{team}} is fourth with 64 points, how many points ahead is {{team}}?

options.text: 5 points
8 points
3 points

explanation.correct: Right. Check the table: the goal is to know your team's actual gap to the team below.
explanation.incorrect: Read the table: fourth on 64, fifth on 61, so three-point gap.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're fourth but only on goal difference.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is averaging two points per game. Is that title-form pace?

scene.alt: A team has played 30 games and won 20, drawn 0, lost 10, for 60 points. Their PPG is 2.0. A title challenger usually averages 2.5+ points per game.

explanation.correct: Right. Two points per game over 38 games = 76 points, which is usually enough to contend; 2.5+ is champion pace.
explanation.incorrect: Two points per game means 76 points over a 38-game season, which competes for the title most years.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Goals for minus goals against: if you've scored 45 and conceded 30, your goal difference is +15.
explanation.incorrect: Goals scored minus goals conceded: the top tiebreaker when teams are level on points.

payload.prompt: Two teams have 60 points. Team A has a goal difference of +10. Team B has +8. Who is ranked higher?

options.text: Team B, alphabetically first
Team A, goal difference is the tiebreaker
It depends on the league rules

explanation.correct: Right. When points are equal, goal difference decides the ranking. Team A's +10 beats Team B's +8.
explanation.incorrect: Goal difference—goals scored minus goals conceded—breaks ties first. Same points, better goal difference wins the position.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We're third but only on head-to-head with second.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Same points and goal difference as second, so head-to-head is the next tiebreaker
Only the head-to-head match decides the league
She thinks the ranking is unfair
The league hasn't played yet

payload.translation: Her team and second place are locked on points and goal difference; the next tiebreaker (head-to-head result or goals scored in games between them) decides the ranking.

followUps.line: What's the head-to-head record between you and second?
followUps.why: Shows you understand how tiebreakers work.

followUps.line: How many points back is fourth?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It's fine to ask her to explain the table tiebreakers.

lessons.title: The fixture that matters
lessons.objective: You can explain why this week's match matters and what's at stake for {{team}}.

payload.prompt: {{team}} trails by one point with three games left. This week: second place. Why does this matter?

options.text: It's the most glamorous fixture
A win puts them top and head-to-head advantage over the direct rival
It has the biggest attendance

explanation.correct: Right. In a title race, games against your closest rivals are decisive. A win flips the race and gives you a head-to-head edge.
explanation.incorrect: A win against second place is title-critical: you go top, gain head-to-head and psychological momentum.

payload.prompt: {{team}} has 32 points, five games left. Team below has 28. How many points makes safety?

options.text: 38 (one more win)
39 (one more win is likely safe)
36 (usually enough to stay up)

explanation.correct: Close. At 36 points with multiple games still to play, {{team}} is usually safe; every league is different.
explanation.incorrect: In most leagues, 36 points is enough to stay up, so {{team}} needs to gain four more from five games.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: It's a derby this week. Form goes out the window.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The usual rankings don't matter in derbies
The match is unpredictable because of the rivalry
One team is too good to lose
Derbies decide the whole season

payload.translation: Derbies between local rivals are so charged with emotion and pride that the better team on paper often doesn't win; rivalries can upset the expected result.

followUps.line: What's the head-to-head record in this derby?
followUps.why: Shows you know derby history matters.

followUps.line: How many of your team's worst losses have come in derbies?
followUps.why: Opens a conversation about the intensity.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to know the derby history; asking her about it is perfect.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We play them when we're chasing, they play us when they're safe. Fixture congestion nightmare.

payload.question: What is she frustrated about?

options.text: The timing of the fixture hurts her team's title push or survival fight
The opponent is resting while her team is desperate
The match is scheduled too late in the season
Ticket prices are too high

payload.translation: Her team chases the title or fights relegation when they're already tired, while the opponent can rest players because they're secure. The fixture list hands an unfair advantage.

followUps.line: How many games in a week do they have?
Who else do they play in that stretch?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Fixture scheduling is genuinely difficult; agreeing that it's unfair is a real observation.

payload.prompt: {{team}} chases the title; their derby rival is midtable. What does midtable gain from this game?

options.text: Nothing, {{team}} is too good
A chance to derail the title race and hand rivals an advantage in the chase
Three points and a memorable moment

explanation.correct: Right. Even if a derby opponent is out of the race, knocking a title contender off pace by two points can reshape the whole season.
explanation.incorrect: A spoiler result against a title contender is massive: it's three points for them and dent to the leader's push.

lessons.title: Injury and lineup news
lessons.objective: You can explain what an injury or lineup change means for {{team}}'s approach this week.

payload.prompt: {{team}}'s main striker is out with a hamstring injury. They have two games in five days. Why is this timing critical?

options.text: One-off bad luck; they'll be fine without him
Fixture congestion means they can't rest him and find form before the second game
Playing two games in five days let's him heal faster

explanation.correct: Right. Two games in five days with a key player out means they're stretched thin on creativity and finishing.
explanation.incorrect: Fixture congestion paired with injury news means fatigue and lack of creative options; the timing hurts most.

payload.prompt: Three players are doubtful but training. One is your best centre-back. Do you risk him?

situation.narrative: You are the manager with two games in three days.

options.label: Bench him and start the backup
options.consequence: You protect him for the league game; the backup gains experience.
considerations: Title race is more important than the cup
Risk of re-injury is high in back-to-back games

options.label: Play him in both games
options.consequence: He re-injures in game one and you lose him for weeks or months.
considerations: Two games in three days with a doubtful player is too risky

options.label: Play him only in the cup to rest him for league
options.consequence: Cup is important but you get him a lighter load; risky if the backup is exposed.
considerations: Cup experience is fine but the league title matters more

payload.expertNote: Managers balance competition importance, injury risk and squad depth. The league title usually wins.
payload.sayThisLine: He trained but the medics say hold him. Title race can't wait for him to heal wrong.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Doubtful to play. That means he'll probably go, right?

payload.question: Is she right?

options.text: Doubtful means likely to play if the match is important
Doubtful means uncertain; he might play or might sit out
Doubtful usually means he won't play
Injury news is always obvious

payload.translation: Doubtful is the middle ground between out and probable: the injury (strain, minor tear, knock) is not severe enough to rule him out, but he's not certain to start.

followUps.why: That's how you gauge if doubtful means he'll go.

followUps.line: Who plays if he doesn't make it?
followUps.why: Shows you're thinking about the backup plan.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Injury reports are vague by design; teams keep cards close. Asking what the fans think is fair.

payload.prompt: {{team}} has three games in seven days. The manager makes five changes for the second game (a cup match). Why?

options.text: The second game is a chance to rotate and keep legs fresh for the third game
The first game didn't go well
The cup is less important than league matches

explanation.correct: Right. Three games in seven days kills legs; rotating in the less critical game keeps your best players sharp for the league.
explanation.incorrect: Fixture congestion forces rotation. Use the cup match or the least critical game to give regulars a breather.

payload.template: {{status}} means the player is expected to play; {{status2}} means it's uncertain.

explanation.correct: Right. Probable = likely to play. Doubtful = coin flip. Out = will definitely miss.
explanation.incorrect: Probable means trained and likely to start; doubtful means tested but could go either way.

lessons.title: Transfer news decoder
lessons.objective: You can tell rumour from confirmed news and read a 'here we go' moment.

payload.prompt: Transfer news: tabloid report, sports journalist, and club statement. Which is confirmed?

options.text: The tabloid is always first
The club statement is official; 'here we go' from a trusted reporter is as good
All three mean the same thing

explanation.correct: Right. A club statement is official. A trusted reporter's 'here we go' carries weight; tabloids are gossip.
explanation.incorrect: Official: club statement or a top reporter like Fabrizio Romano with 'here we go'. Tabloids = rumour until confirmed.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: It's deadline day and there's four hours. He's not getting done now.

payload.question: What's her reasoning?

options.text: Medical checks, paperwork and registration take time even on deadline day
The seller is being difficult
Four hours is enough for a complex transfer
A transfer requires club statements

payload.translation: Late-window deals need medical exams, paperwork, registration and the league's OK; four hours is tight for a big deal unless it's already agreed.

followUps.line: Has the player's club confirmed they agreed a fee?
What's left to do besides medicals?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Deadline day chaos is real; asking why something is stalled is a fair question.

payload.prompt: Contract ends June 30. July 1: he joins anyone free. This move is called?

options.text: A free transfer or out-of-contract move
A loan
A release clause

explanation.correct: Right. When a contract expires, the player is out of contract and can join anyone free of charge.
explanation.incorrect: Contract expiry means the player is free to go. After his contract ends, no club can stop him signing elsewhere without a fee.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Ten different websites say he's done. But no club statement.

payload.question: Should she believe it?

options.text: If many sources agree, it's probably true
Multiple rumours don't equal confirmation; a club or trusted reporter's 'here we go' matters most
Rumours spread faster than facts
One club statement beats ten rumours

payload.translation: Rumours echo across sites even when they're wrong. Only a club statement, a trusted reporter's 'here we go', or official news counts as confirmed.

followUps.line: Has anyone official—club or reporter—said 'here we go'?
Has the player's current club denied it?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rumour season is fun but stressful; staying sceptical is smart.

payload.prompt: Your star winger's contract ends in six months. A big club offers him a deal. Do you sell now or let him leave free?

situation.narrative: You are the club's sporting director.

options.label: Sell for €30m and reinvest
options.consequence: You get €30m instead of zero; you use it to strengthen the squad and fight for Europe.
considerations: A player who wants to leave is a distraction

options.label: Keep him until his contract ends
options.consequence: You get no fee, he leaves free, and you lose leverage.

options.label: Loan him out and sell in the summer
options.consequence: You keep him off the pitch and his value stays high for the summer window.
considerations: Risky if his value drops during a loan

payload.expertNote: Clubs balance sentiment with reality: a sale for less than market is often smarter than a free exit.
payload.sayThisLine: He wants out, so thirty million now beats zero in the summer.

lessons.title: Title race and relegation maths
lessons.objective: You can calculate what {{team}} needs from the run-in to win or survive.

payload.prompt: {{team}} has 65 points, 5 games left. Leader has 68. Points needed to win?

options.text: 10 (three wins)
12 (four wins)
15 (five wins)

explanation.correct: Right. {{team}} wins four (12 points) to reach 77, which usually beats 75 (the leader's max).
explanation.incorrect: If {{team}} wins four of five games they get 77 points; the leader maxes out at 75, so 12 points does it.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is 18th with 25 points. How many more points typically guarantee survival?

explanation.correct: Close. 11 more points = 36 total, which is usually safe; one-two wins over the run-in.
explanation.incorrect: Around 36 points is the survival line in most leagues; {{team}} needs roughly 11 more points from remaining games.

payload.prompt: {{team}} plays the leader at 70 points each, three games left. Win is worth how much?

options.text: Just three points, like any other win
Six points (three for you, minus three you'd lose if you didn't win)
Priceless, it's the whole season

explanation.correct: Right. A win gives you +3 and costs them -0, so the net gap is 6 points. Head-to-head is worth double.
explanation.incorrect: When you play the leader: a win is three points for you and zero for them, so the swing is six points in gap.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The run-in is brutal. We've got three of the top four coming up.

payload.question: What's she worried about?

options.text: Playing strong teams in the final stretch hurts the title chances
The remaining games are all very difficult
Three games at once
The season is almost over

payload.translation: The run-in is the last set of fixtures; a brutal run-in means tough opponents when {{team}} needs to win. Easy run-ins let you catch up.

followUps.line: What's your worst-case scenario from those three games?
When do you play the bottom half?
followUps.why: Shows you're thinking about winnable games.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Worrying about the fixture list is totally fair; fixture luck is real.

payload.prompt: {{team}} trails the leader by 5 points with 4 games left. What's the minimum gap if the leader wins all four?

explanation.correct: Right. Leader on 12 more points (48 total), {{team}} stays at their current tally, so 17-point gap.
explanation.incorrect: Leader gains 12 points (4 wins); the gap becomes 5 + 12 = 17 points. {{team}} can't catch up.

lessons.title: What is everyone talking about
lessons.objective: You can name and explain the story fans are talking about today.

payload.prompt: The manager is under pressure after two losses in six games. What do fans mean by 'sack race'?

options.text: A running event for fans
Speculation about whether the manager will be fired
A race to the bottom of the table

explanation.correct: Right. 'In the sack race' means the manager's job is in danger; odds shift as results change.
explanation.incorrect: Sack race is the speculation game: will the club fire the manager? Betting odds and media heat move together.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: There's an international break next week and three of our best players are away. Nightmare.

payload.question: What's the problem?

options.text: Her team loses match fitness while other teams rest
International matches don't count for the league
Players travel far and come back tired or injured
The league pauses but her team doesn't

payload.translation: International breaks pause the league while national teams play. Her best players are away and often return fatigued or injured, and the club loses time to train together.

followUps.line: Do you have a game right after they get back?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: International breaks are genuinely disruptive; it's a real fixture-list problem.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: VAR checked that for four minutes for nothing. It was never going to change.

payload.question: What's she frustrated about?

options.text: A long VAR review that didn't overturn the on-field call
VAR reviewing an incident that wasn't serious
VAR always makes wrong calls
Four minutes is too long for any review

payload.translation: VAR spent four minutes reviewing and ultimately kept the original call. She feels the review was unnecessary or that the ref should have trusted the on-field read.

followUps.why: Lets her explain what she saw.

followUps.line: Did you think it was the right call in the end?
followUps.why: Invites her to discuss the decision.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Frustration with VAR pace is totally valid; 'clear and obvious' is genuinely subjective.

payload.title: Why is everyone talking about this?
payload.setting: She brings up a story from the past week—maybe a managerial rumour or an injury in an international match.

exchanges.theirMessage: The manager is definitely leaving. Everyone knows it.

replies.text: Has the club said anything? Or is it media speculation?
replies.theirResponse: Speculation so far, but it feels done.

payload.closingNote: Managerial pressure is a huge story; distinguishing rumour from reality helps.

payload.title: Injury during the break
payload.setting: She mentions a player who got injured on international duty and missed the next {{team}} game.

exchanges.theirMessage: He got injured at the international break and now we're playing {{team}} without him.

replies.text: Ouch. Was it a contact injury or overuse from the extra game?
replies.theirResponse: Tackle. Unnecessary too, the match was decided.
replies.coachNote: Asks for detail and shows empathy.

replies.theirResponse: I mean, yeah, but he loves playing for his country.

payload.closingNote: International-break injuries are a sore point; asking details is sympathetic.
